Retinol Equivalents Vitamin A is ingested either as pre-formed vitamin A (retinol or retinyl 
ester), or a beta-carotene that can be split into retinol in the intestine. Beta-carotene is the most 
abundant carotenoid present in green, yellow, and orange fruits and vegetables. Due to inefficient 
conversion, 12 µg of beta-carotene in food yields only about 1 µg retinol, and therefore a serving 
of food that contains 12 µg of beta-carotene is said to contain 1 µg RAE (retinol activity equivalent; 
older literature uses a similar concept with the abbreviation RE, for retinol equivalent). Because 
other carotenoids are even less efficiently converted to retinol, 1 µg RAE equates to 24 µg of these 
other carotenoid species.
International units (IU) are also used to express the amount of vitamin A in supplements and 
occasionally in foods; 100 IU of retinol in supplements translates to 30 µg RAE, while 100 IU of 
beta-carotene equates to 5 µg RAE.
